title: NotesApp threat model and risk analysis
basis: Current working tree, including the Session 3 AES-GCM comment homework

boundaries.name: Browser / network to Flask
boundaries.reason: Credentials, cookies, JWTs and all request parameters come from a client outside server control. The current deployment uses HTTP.

boundaries.name: Application or host network to PostgreSQL
boundaries.reason: Database authentication and SQL separate application input from stored records. The published port also creates a path that bypasses Flask.

boundaries.name: Stored comment text to browser execution
boundaries.reason: The browser must treat returned comments as data. Disabled Jinja escaping lets stored content cross into executable page markup.

boundaries.name: Admin form input to OS command interpreter
boundaries.reason: An authenticated host field remains untrusted. shell=True interprets it as shell syntax with the web process privileges.

boundaries.name: Web container to Docker engine and mounted host project
boundaries.reason: Docker socket access grants control of the Linux Docker engine. The writable /host mount exposes project files, including the original AES key file. On Docker Desktop, Linux engine control does not itself prove Windows kernel administrator access.

boundaries.name: Application to secret and audit storage
boundaries.reason: Key loading and audit writes cross a storage access boundary. This is a logical protection boundary, not a separate container. Root execution and permissive log/config/backup permissions weaken its enforcement.

flows.from: D5 Seed SQL mount / Docker initialization
flows.data: First-volume initialization SQL, including seed users and plaintext comments before the startup migration

threats.name: Unsigned or weakly signed JWT identity
threats.asset: Student records and authenticated API identity
threats.scenario: A caller supplies an unsigned JWT identity. The API accepts alg:none and only checks that an identity exists, then decrypts the requested note.
threats.precondition: Ability to send HTTP requests. A valid account is unnecessary for the unsigned-token path.
threats.likelihood_reason: The API directly accepts unsigned identity from public requests, with no account or secret prerequisite.
threats.impact_reason: The attacker can obtain arbitrary plaintext grades/comments through the API. Bearer identity alone does not satisfy the session-only teacher/admin checks.
threats.fix: Use a maintained JWT verifier, an explicit algorithm allowlist and a strong separate key. Validate exp/iss/aud and resolve user state server-side. Apply object authorization after authentication.

threats.name: SQL injection at login
threats.scenario: Untrusted login strings become SQL syntax. A changed query can return another identity or operate with the application database role.
threats.likelihood_reason: The public login directly concatenates both inputs without binding parameters.
threats.impact_reason: A returned admin identity enables privileged routes. The runtime application database role is also a superuser, increasing database-wide damage.
threats.fix: Bind username with a parameterized lookup, verify a password hash separately, suppress raw query errors, and give the application a limited non-superuser database role.

threats.name: Public Flask session signing key
threats.asset: Teacher/admin authority and all managed records
threats.scenario: A person who knows the public development signing key can construct a session asserting an admin or teacher role. Privileged routes trust those cookie fields.
threats.precondition: Access to the public repository/configuration and HTTP requests.
threats.likelihood_reason: The signing key is committed and is also the application fallback, so no key guessing is required.
threats.impact_reason: A forged admin session can manage users and reach the unsafe command runner. This is a chained impact, not a claim that alg:none JWTs directly log into admin pages.
threats.fix: Load a new random session key from separate secret storage, fail startup if absent, invalidate old sessions, and re-read current user/role from the database before privileged actions.

threats.name: Teacher changes another teacher's records
threats.scenario: An ordinary teacher submits a note_id from another class or creates a note for an unrelated class/student. The write only tests the teacher role.
threats.precondition: A teacher account or equivalent forged session.
threats.likelihood_reason: There is no check of classes.teacher_id, note ownership or enrollment on the server.
threats.impact_reason: Any teacher can alter grades outside their scope and export other classes. AES-GCM encrypts the unauthorized write successfully.
threats.fix: Scope every teacher read/export/write by the authenticated teacher's class ownership. Check enrollment for new notes and reject changes to another teacher's note.

threats.name: State-changing requests lack CSRF verification
threats.asset: Grades, user accounts and admin operations
threats.scenario: An attacker induces an authenticated browser to submit an unwanted state-changing request where its cookies accompany the request.
threats.precondition: A signed-in teacher/admin and a browser/site context that sends the session cookie. Actual exploitability depends on SameSite behavior and site/origin relationship.
threats.likelihood_reason: No server-side token check exists, but modern browser cookie restrictions can block some cross-site POST cases.
threats.impact_reason: A successful unwanted request can alter grades, delete/create users or trigger a privileged command.
threats.fix: Validate CSRF tokens on all state-changing routes. Set explicit Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookie policy under HTTPS and check Origin as an additional control.

threats.name: Stored comment executes in the browser
threats.asset: Browser session authority and displayed records
threats.scenario: A teacher or compromised writer stores executable markup in a comment. After authenticated decryption, the student/teacher page renders it with escaping disabled.
threats.precondition: Comment write access and a victim who opens the affected page.
threats.likelihood_reason: The application intentionally disables escaping on both comment views.
threats.impact_reason: Code runs in the victim's application origin and can issue requests as that browser. HttpOnly does not stop same-origin requests or access to the JWT embedded in the page.
threats.fix: Enable escaping for plain comments. If rich text is necessary, apply a maintained strict HTML sanitizer and deploy CSP as an additional control.

threats.name: Database edits bypass the comment's limited AAD scope
threats.asset: Grade integrity and the association of comments to students/classes
threats.scenario: A database writer changes grade, student_id or class_id without changing the comment ciphertext. The AAD contains note.id only. Restoring an older valid ciphertext for the same id also passes authentication.
threats.precondition: Database write access through another vulnerability or a privileged insider.
threats.likelihood_reason: The attacker first needs database write authority, rather than only a normal browser account.
threats.impact_reason: A valid tag proves this comment and note id match, but does not prove the grade/owner metadata or freshness. A changed owner can cause plaintext to reach the wrong student.
threats.fix: Restrict database writers, enforce record authorization, maintain protected change history, and bind stable owner/class context where the application design permits. Use a trusted version/history control to detect rollback.

threats.name: Grade changes have insufficient audit evidence
threats.asset: Accountability for grading and user administration
threats.scenario: A privileged user denies changing a grade or user. The local log lacks old/new values and reliable identity, admin user changes lack an event, and writable log storage permits alteration.
threats.precondition: An authorized/compromised account and, for log deletion, file write access.
threats.likelihood_reason: The information missing from the existing logger cannot establish a complete transaction history.
threats.impact_reason: The institution cannot reliably reconstruct disputed changes. Missing evidence makes investigation and recovery harder, even though it is not by itself a grade change.
threats.fix: Write structured audit events containing verified actor, target id, old/new values, time, outcome and request id to protected central storage. Limit readers and define retention without recording secrets.

threats.name: Any student reads another student's decrypted note
threats.scenario: A signed-in student changes the note id in the API URL. The query only filters by id and the response decrypts the comment.
threats.precondition: An ordinary student account. Token forgery is a separate alternative in S01.
threats.likelihood_reason: Predictable integer ids and an explicit missing ownership check make cross-student reads simple.
threats.impact_reason: Students can read other students' records. Encryption at rest does not restrict what an application decrypts for a caller.
threats.fix: Check note.student_id against the verified student identity and check class ownership for teacher access. Return a consistent denial response and test cross-account reads.

threats.name: Plain HTTP exposes credentials and responses
threats.asset: Passwords, sessions and plaintext grades/comments in transit
threats.scenario: A network observer on a reachable deployment reads or modifies HTTP requests/responses, including credentials and server-decrypted comments.
threats.precondition: A position on the traffic path. Local localhost traffic has lower exposure than a campus/public deployment.
threats.likelihood_reason: HTTP is explicit, but a useful interception position is an additional condition.
threats.impact_reason: Stolen credentials/cookies can compromise privileged users. The encrypted database column does not protect network responses.
threats.fix: Use a configured TLS reverse proxy, redirect HTTP, enable HSTS after deployment checks and mark session cookies Secure. Verify that the HTTP backend is not independently published.

threats.name: Direct database access reveals plaintext credentials
threats.asset: All accounts, grades and database availability
threats.scenario: A reachable database client uses the public teaching database credential on the published port, or an existing SQL/DB foothold reads users.password. Seed credentials and image backups also contain plaintext passwords.
threats.precondition: Network/host reachability of PostgreSQL, a database foothold, or access to image/backup files. Firewall and routing determine remote reachability.
threats.likelihood_reason: The credential and port mapping are visible, but access through the host firewall is not assumed proven.
threats.impact_reason: Passwords, grades and all records are exposed, and the runtime database role is superuser. An isolated database dump still lacks the AES key, so encrypted comment text is not automatically readable from that dump alone.
threats.fix: Remove the published database port unless needed locally, restrict network access, use a separate limited app role and managed secrets, hash passwords, and remove credential-bearing image backups.

threats.name: Web process compromise exposes the AES key
threats.scenario: Code executing as the web process reads the runtime secret or the original key under /host/.secrets/comment_key.b64, then combines it with ciphertext. The current broad writable host mount also permits key replacement.
threats.precondition: Web process code execution or sufficiently privileged host/project file access.
threats.likelihood_reason: A separate compromise is needed, but the command-injection chain provides a concrete route.
threats.impact_reason: A stolen key defeats comment confidentiality across records and permits valid re-encryption. Merely excluding the file from Git does not protect it from the running web process.
threats.fix: Remove broad host mounts and command execution, apply least privilege and narrow secret delivery, separately protect key backups, and plan controlled rotation/re-encryption after a key compromise.

threats.name: Unbounded requests and logs exhaust resources
threats.scenario: Repeated login/API/export requests consume connections and CPU. Each login attempt can append to an unrotated log until storage fills. The deployment specifies no application rate limits or container resource limits.
threats.precondition: HTTP access and enough repeated traffic. No load attack was performed during this review.
threats.likelihood_reason: Public endpoints allocate work without quotas, and the development server is the active serving process.
threats.impact_reason: The service can become unavailable or slow and logs can fill the disk. The exact saturation point is unmeasured.
threats.fix: Use a production WSGI service, request/connection limits, login throttling, export pagination, container CPU/memory quotas, log rotation and monitoring.

threats.name: Unreadable encrypted comment blocks service startup
threats.scenario: A database writer corrupts an encrypted comment or a key file is lost/replaced. The migration authenticates every encrypted comment before starting Flask and stops on a failure.
threats.precondition: Database write access or key/storage failure, followed by restart for the startup scenario.
threats.likelihood_reason: This requires a separate write/failure condition, not an unauthenticated API call alone.
threats.impact_reason: One bad record can prevent startup. Rejecting invalid data is the correct authentication behavior; the availability risk lies in startup coupling and recovery readiness.
threats.fix: Protect and separately back up the database/key, test restore procedures, report the affected record without leaking plaintext, and design controlled quarantine/recovery while continuing to reject unauthenticated data.

threats.name: Admin shell injection reaches Docker engine control
threats.asset: Container, Linux Docker engine, project files and secrets
threats.scenario: An admin-capable caller inserts shell syntax in host. The command runs as root, and the process can reach the Docker socket and writable host project. SQL login bypass or the public session key can provide the admin session first.
threats.precondition: An admin session, obtained legitimately or through S02/S03. Docker daemon/socket availability as configured.
threats.likelihood_reason: The shell and root configuration are explicit and the public session key makes the admin prerequisite reachable without a private secret.
threats.impact_reason: Code execution can control the Linux Docker engine and alter mounted project data or retrieve keys. Native Windows kernel takeover was not tested or claimed.
threats.fix: Remove the ping feature or strictly validate an IP and run an argument list with shell=False. Remove socket and broad host mounts, run non-root, drop capabilities and restrict writable paths.

threats.name: Application database role has superuser privileges
threats.asset: Database administration and all application records
threats.scenario: An attacker with an SQL/database foothold inherits the application's superuser role instead of only the permissions needed to read and manage authorized records.
threats.precondition: Another flaw such as SQL injection or access to the published database with its configured credential.
threats.likelihood_reason: This is a privilege amplifier after a database foothold. Runtime read-only inspection confirmed rolsuper=true.
threats.impact_reason: The foothold can affect the whole PostgreSQL instance and all stored data. A server process or host compromise is not automatically assumed.
threats.fix: Create a separate non-superuser application role with only required table/sequence permissions. Keep schema/migration/owner accounts outside the request-handling process.

priorities.title: Parameterized login and limited database role
priorities.decision: Fix the unauthenticated SQL entry first because it can bypass every intended role and reach an overprivileged database.
steps: Parameterize a username-only lookup and verify a password hash separately. Migrate existing passwords with a controlled reset/hash procedure.
Remove raw query errors from browser responses and keep useful internal diagnostics.
Create a non-superuser application role. Keep schema ownership and startup migration privileges separate from request handling.
acceptance: Normal student/teacher/admin login works. Quote-like inputs are bound as data and cannot select a different identity.
The request-handling DB role has rolsuper=false, cannot CREATE/DROP schema objects, and has only required table/sequence privileges.
Password columns no longer contain reusable plaintext passwords and the login error response has no SQL details.
priorities.residual: 8/25 is a target after the whole fix, not an observed result. Removing database administration rights still leaves potentially serious effects on application records. Application authorization and compromised legitimate accounts need separate controls.

priorities.title: Remove shell execution and Docker host access
priorities.decision: Contain the largest blast radius next. This also removes a route to the AES key and the host project.
steps: Remove /admin/ping if it is unnecessary. If retained, accept only a strictly parsed IP and invoke ping with an argument list and shell=False.
Remove both /var/run/docker.sock and .:/host mounts. Supply only required files with narrow, preferably read-only mounts.
Run the web process as a dedicated non-root user, drop capabilities, restrict writable paths and apply resource limits.
acceptance: The removed route cannot execute a command, or malformed host input fails validation before a mocked process runner receives it.
Runtime UID is nonzero. Docker socket and broad /host paths are absent from container mounts.
AES-GCM save/read still works through the narrow secret mount. The application cannot write to the host project or control the Docker engine.
priorities.residual: 8/25 is a target, not a completed hardening result. A compromised application may still access its own runtime key and authorized database operations.

priorities.title: Replace the public session key and verify current roles
priorities.decision: Remove the direct cookie-forgery path into privileged web routes. Authentication keys and AES keys must remain separate.
steps: Generate a strong random session key in protected secret storage, remove the public fallback and fail startup when the key is absent.
Invalidate sessions signed with the old key. Re-read the acting user and current role from the database before privileged actions.
Replace permissive JWT verification with a maintained verifier, a fixed allowed algorithm and required lifetime/issuer/audience checks. Check each object's permissions separately.
acceptance: Cookies signed with the old development key cannot authenticate to teacher/admin routes.
Missing key configuration fails startup. Student/admin role changes or account deletion affect subsequent requests.
Unsigned, tampered, expired and incorrectly scoped JWTs fail. Ordinary legitimate sessions continue to work after users sign in again.
priorities.residual: 5/25 is a target. Theft of the new signing key is still serious, and fixing authentication alone does not remove I01/T01 object authorization flaws.
